Plan by age · Stage 5 of 5

Ages 63–65: Medicare countdown

Medicare at 65 is the last big deadline before retirement settles into a routine. Income from two years earlier sets your Medicare premiums, so the planning starts at 63. Missing the enrollment window can mean penalties that last as long as you have Medicare.

It is also time to finish the paperwork that protects everything else: wills, beneficiaries and powers of attorney. Then you can turn savings into a paycheck you can count on.

Birthdays that matter

  • 63The last year of the super catch-up, and the first tax year Medicare looks back to when it sets your premiums at 65. Medicare.gov: 2026 Medicare costs (incl. IRMAA table)
  • 65Medicare's Initial Enrollment Period runs 7 months around your 65th birthday month. Medicare.gov: When can I sign up?
  • 65An extra $6,000 senior deduction per eligible person for tax years 2025 through 2028. IRS: Enhanced deduction for seniors

IRMAA: income at 63 sets premiums at 65

What's happening

Medicare Part B and Part D premiums rise in tiers when income on your tax return from two years earlier is above set thresholds. The return for the year you turn 63 sets the premiums you pay at 65.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Paying a higher IRMAA tier for a year in exchange for a larger Roth conversion.

Common mistakes

  • Selling a business or a home at 63 without checking the IRMAA effect two years later.
  • Not appealing after a work stoppage or other life-changing event.

Key numbers for 2026

  • $109,000 / $218,000IRMAA starts above2026 Part B premiums use 2024 income (single / married filing jointly).Source: Medicare.gov: 2026 Medicare costs (incl. IRMAA table)
  • $202.90–$689.90/moPart B premium range2026, standard premium to the top IRMAA tier.Source: CMS: 2026 Medicare Parts A and B premiums and deductibles

Enrolling in Medicare at 65

What's happening

Your Initial Enrollment Period starts 3 months before your 65th birthday month and ends 3 months after. If you are still covered by an active employer's plan you may be able to wait, but the rules are strict.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Original Medicare plus Medigap versus Medicare Advantage.
  • Enroll at 65 or delay Part B because of employer coverage.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming COBRA or retiree coverage lets you delay Part B. It usually does not.
  • Contributing to an HSA in the months Medicare covers retroactively.

Key numbers for 2026

  • $202.90/moPart B standard premium2026, with a $283 yearly deductible.Source: CMS: 2026 Medicare Parts A and B premiums and deductibles
  • $1,736Part A hospital deductible2026, per benefit period.Source: CMS: 2026 Medicare Parts A and B premiums and deductibles
  • 10% per 12 monthsPart B late penaltyAdded for each full 12-month period you could have had Part B but did not, for as long as you have Part B.Source: Medicare.gov: Avoid late enrollment penalties

Estate basics and beneficiaries

What's happening

Most families never owe federal estate tax, but every family needs the paperwork. Beneficiary forms decide who gets retirement accounts and life insurance, whatever the will says. Most heirs other than a spouse must empty an inherited IRA within 10 years.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Gifting now versus leaving money at death.
  • Whether a trust is worth the cost for your situation.

Common mistakes

  • Naming 'my estate' as the beneficiary, which can force faster taxable withdrawals.
  • Assuming a will controls retirement accounts.

Key numbers for 2026

  • $15,000,000Estate and gift tax exclusion2026, per person.Source: IRS: What's new, estate and gift tax
  • $19,000Annual gift exclusion2026, per recipient.Source: IRS: What's new, estate and gift tax

Final readiness check and a retirement paycheck

What's happening

Turning savings into a reliable paycheck is a different job from saving. You need an order for withdrawals, a cash reserve for bad markets and a plan that holds up if you live into your 90s.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • How much to spend in the early, active years.
  • Whether to buy guaranteed income for part of your spending.

Common mistakes

  • Spending from whichever account is easiest instead of the one that is cheapest in tax.
  • Planning to an average life expectancy rather than a long one.

Key numbers for 2026

  • $6,000 per personSenior deductionAge 65+, tax years 2025–2028; phases out above $75,000 / $150,000 of income (single / joint).Source: IRS: Enhanced deduction for seniors
  • age 73Required minimum distributionsPlan withdrawals now so RMDs do not force large taxable income later.Source: IRS: Required minimum distribution FAQs
